claims.claim_text: Encrypted chats still require trusting providers (summary thesis).
claims.evidence_quote: you're trusting their reputation, jurisdiction, business model, and past behavior rather than cryptographically verifiable guarantees
claims.reasoning: Summary synthesis of the piece's bottom line; identical meaning.

claims.claim_text: Only client-held keys minimize that trust.
claims.evidence_quote: Security-conscious people prefer client-side encryption ... systems that minimize trust
claims.reasoning: Matches the source minimize-trust recommendation.

claims.claim_text: E2EE means device-to-device secrecy.
claims.evidence_quote: data is encrypted on sender's device and then decrypted on receiver's device without it ever being decrypted along the way is in fact the definition of it
claims.reasoning: Definition restated with identical meaning.

claims.claim_text: Users need provider exclusion, not just transit safety.
claims.evidence_quote: one wants E2EE so that no one can access the data outside the sender and receivers, and in particular the provider
claims.reasoning: Captures the source distinction between man-in-the-middle purpose and provider-exclusion purpose.

claims.claim_text: This is a non-expert end-user inquiry from a conversation with Omid.
claims.evidence_quote: This came out of a conversation with Omid. DISCLAIMER: I'm not a security expert ... as an end user
claims.reasoning: Both the Omid origin and the non-expert disclaimer match.

claims.claim_text: Metadata (network, frequency, volume, timing) still aids interpretation.
claims.evidence_quote: they know your network, the frequency and amount of communication, times of communication etc
claims.reasoning: All four metadata kinds preserved.

claims.claim_text: If implemented as claimed with no secret backdoors, Meta cannot access message content.
claims.evidence_quote: if they have implemented the things in the way they claim they have, and if they haven't implemented other backdoors that they have kept secret, then yes, they can't access that data
claims.reasoning: Conditional structure and can't outcome preserved exactly.

claims.claim_text: The app is not open source and not really auditable; external audits cannot prove the negative.
claims.evidence_quote: the app is not open source, and hence not really auditable ... they can never claim it can't access those data
claims.reasoning: Both the closed-source cause and the negative-certainty limit preserved, negations intact.

claims.claim_text: Business model, the 2021 ad-sharing policy, and the 2019 plaintext failure imply near-certain access.
claims.evidence_quote: when you think about what the company's business is, their 2021 privacy policy changes ... and previous security failures like storing hundreds of millions of passwords in plaintext, you can almost be certain that they can, and they do access them
claims.reasoning: All three evidence legs plus the almost-be-certain qualifier preserved as near-certain implication.

claims.claim_text: Smoking-gun test: whether history is reachable on a new device with no manual key transfer.
claims.evidence_quote: a smoking gun is whether the platform/app is able to backup your data. Whether you can access your history across devices without manually linking them somehow
claims.reasoning: Test definition restated with identical meaning.

claims.claim_text: Locker plus receiver-only master key analogy; server key access equals a public billboard copy.
claims.evidence_quote: I think of encryption as locking something and having a key ... if at any time, Facebook has access to it, it is as if you've locked your door and left a copy at the local farmers market billboard
claims.reasoning: Analogy compressed with the billboard consequence intact.

claims.claim_text: The WhatsApp server stores encrypted history and hands keys to devices it authenticates.
claims.evidence_quote: the server stores encrypted message history and maintains mappings ... When you add a new device, the server authenticates it and provides it with the keys needed to decrypt your message history
claims.reasoning: Storage plus server-authenticated key-grant mechanism preserved.

claims.claim_text: Device lists and security codes rely on honest server reporting; a rogue device could be hidden.
claims.evidence_quote: Their claimed safeguards (device lists you can check, security codes you can verify) all depend on the server honestly reporting what devices exist - but since they control that server, they could simply hide a rogue device
claims.reasoning: Safeguards, honesty dependence, and hiding consequence all preserved.

claims.claim_text: Proton generates the private key in-browser, wrapping it with bcrypt and AES-256.
claims.evidence_quote: your private key is generated in your browser, then encrypted with your password using bcrypt and AES-256
claims.reasoning: Generation site and both algorithms match exactly.

claims.claim_text: Six-step login: type, bcrypt with server salt, authenticate, fetch key, decrypt locally, read.
claims.evidence_quote: You type your password ... hashes the password using bcrypt (with a salt provided by Proton's server) ... sent to Proton to authenticate ... sends your encrypted private key back ... uses your original password to decrypt ... Now you can read your emails
claims.reasoning: All six enumerated source steps compressed in order.

claims.claim_text: Hashing authenticates one-way; encryption protects two-way under the actual password.
claims.evidence_quote: Hashing (used for authentication): A one-way function ... Encryption (used for your private key): A two-way function ... encrypted with your actual password (not the hash)
claims.reasoning: Both definitions and the actual-password distinction preserved.

claims.claim_text: In theory the seen hash cannot decrypt the password-wrapped key.
claims.evidence_quote: even though they see your hashed password, they can't use that hash to decrypt your encrypted private key
claims.reasoning: Negation and in-theory scope preserved.

claims.claim_text: Counterpoint: malicious client code could capture the typed password before hashing.
claims.evidence_quote: Proton could serve you malicious client code ... that captures your actual password when you type it - before it gets hashed
claims.reasoning: Attack vector and before-hashing timing preserved.

claims.claim_text: Trust requires matching served code, no compelled injection, uncompromised infrastructure.
claims.evidence_quote: The code they're actually serving matches the open-source code ... won't be compelled to inject malicious code ... infrastructure hasn't been compromised
claims.reasoning: All three trust conditions preserved.

claims.claim_text: Proton must steal the password first; WhatsApp grants keys directly.
claims.evidence_quote: Proton doesn't have direct access to your encryption keys in a form they can use - they'd need to actively compromise the client to steal your password first. WhatsApp's architecture doesn't even require that step; the server can directly grant key access
claims.reasoning: The crucial-difference contrast preserved exactly.

claims.claim_text: Signal offers a 30-digit passphrase file, device-to-device transfer, or an unseen 64-character key.
claims.evidence_quote: protected by a 30-digit passphrase ... Direct device-to-device transfer ... encrypted with a 64-character recovery key that Signal never sees
claims.reasoning: All three options with exact figures and the never-sees qualifier.

claims.claim_text: Android backup needs physical transfer; direct transfer needs both devices present.
claims.evidence_quote: physically transfer it to your new device ... Both devices must be physically present and you transfer everything locally
claims.reasoning: Both physical-presence requirements preserved.

claims.claim_text: Zero-knowledge: Signal cannot decrypt backups and cannot help recover a lost key.
claims.evidence_quote: Signal literally cannot decrypt your backups even if they wanted to, and they cannot help you recover them if you lose your recovery key. This is genuinely zero-knowledge architecture
claims.reasoning: Both cannots and the zero-knowledge label preserved.

claims.claim_text: Plaintext password storage cannot be ruled out with certainty.
claims.evidence_quote: we don't know for certain ... Short answer: We don't know for certain
claims.reasoning: Header matches the source short answer verbatim in meaning.

claims.claim_text: Open clients prove sending behavior, never the server's later handling.
claims.evidence_quote: you can confirm that passwords are hashed before transmission. But you cannot verify what happens on the server after your password arrives
claims.reasoning: The can-verify-client versus cannot-verify-server contrast preserved.

claims.claim_text: Facebook logged hundreds of millions of passwords in plaintext for years.
claims.evidence_quote: Facebook disclosed in 2019 that they'd been accidentally logging hundreds of millions of passwords in plaintext in internal logs for years
claims.reasoning: Scale, plaintext mode, and years duration preserved.

claims.claim_text: Adobe leaked password hints in plaintext; weak unsalted MD5 persists at small services.
claims.evidence_quote: Adobe's 2013 breach revealed they stored password hints in plaintext. Many smaller services store passwords in plaintext or use weak hashing like MD5 without salting
claims.reasoning: Both precedents with correct details.

claims.claim_text: Proton password reset destroys old mail, suggesting genuine inability, but proving nothing.
claims.evidence_quote: if you reset your password via email/SMS recovery, you lose access to all your old encrypted emails. This suggests they genuinely can't decrypt your data without your password. But even this isn't proof
claims.reasoning: Evidence, suggestive reading, and isn't-proof limit all preserved.

claims.claim_text: Trust rests on reputation, jurisdiction, business model, behavior, not verifiable guarantees.
claims.evidence_quote: you're trusting the company's reputation, jurisdiction, business model, and past behavior rather than having cryptographically verifiable guarantees
claims.reasoning: Four trust bases plus the rather-than contrast preserved.

claims.claim_text: Three models: escrow (WhatsApp) versus password-wrapped (Proton) versus client-controlled (Signal).
claims.evidence_quote: Server-mediated key escrow ... Password-encrypted server-side key storage ... Client-controlled keys
claims.reasoning: All three source model names mapped to services correctly.

claims.claim_text: Silent rogue device: YES for WhatsApp; NO for Proton and Signal with the client caveat.
claims.evidence_quote: Can the service provider add a device without your knowledge? YES ... NO - but they could serve malicious client code ... NO - they cannot authenticate a device without either your recovery key or physical access
claims.reasoning: Table row values plus the Proton client-code caveat preserved.

claims.claim_text: Checkable: open clients, Wireshark traffic inspection, audits of deployed code.
claims.evidence_quote: Open-source clients ... Network traffic inspection: Tools like Wireshark ... Security audits
claims.reasoning: All three checkable avenues preserved.

claims.claim_text: Uncheckable: running code, later updates, rogue staff, breaches.
claims.evidence_quote: Whether they changed it later ... Rogue employees or breaches ... you can't verify that's what's actually running
claims.reasoning: All four uncheckable items preserved.

claims.claim_text: Good signs: open servers, audits, clean breaches; bad signs: reset-proof data, obscurity, violations.
claims.evidence_quote: Open-source server code ... Independent security audits ... Breach disclosure ... Can reset password and access old data ... Security through obscurity ... History of privacy violations
claims.reasoning: All three good and three bad signs compressed correctly.

claims.claim_text: Facebook 2019: 200-600 million passwords, 20,000-plus searchers, archives from 2012.
claims.evidence_quote: logging between 200-600 million passwords in plaintext ... searchable by over 20,000 Facebook employees, with some archives dating back to 2012
claims.reasoning: All three figures match source exactly.

claims.claim_text: Trust ends only with client-side crypto, zero-knowledge servers, verifiable builds.
claims.evidence_quote: All cryptography happens client-side ... zero-knowledge proof systems ... Server code is open-source AND reproducibly built AND you can verify what's running
claims.reasoning: All three escape conditions preserved.

claims.claim_text: WhatsApp needs whole-infrastructure trust; Proton hashing honesty; Signal key custody.
claims.evidence_quote: WhatsApp: Meta's entire server infrastructure ... Proton Mail: They hash your password properly ... Signal: Much less trust required ... you won't lose your recovery key
claims.reasoning: Applied-table row for each service compressed correctly.

claims.claim_text: Prefer client-side encryption, open source, decentralization, hardware keys like YubiKey.
claims.evidence_quote: Security-conscious people prefer client-side encryption, open-source everything, decentralized systems that minimize trust, and hardware security keys (like YubiKey)
claims.reasoning: Bottom-line recommendation with all four elements and the YubiKey example.

claims.claim_text: Sources: Meta 2021 engineering, Proton key docs, Signal September 2024 backups.
claims.evidence_quote: How WhatsApp enables multi-device capability (Engineering at Meta, July 2021) ... How is the private key stored? ... Introducing Signal Secure Backups (Signal Blog, September 2024)
claims.reasoning: Source list compressed with correct attributions and dates.
